title: House Passes Graham Russia Sanctions Bill 262-159, Putting India in 100% Tariff Crosshairs
excerpt: Named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, the package authorises President Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top importers of Russian energy; the Kremlin said Thursday the move would 'complicate' Ukraine peace efforts.
body:
• The House passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Wednesday by a 262-159 vote, with dozens of Democrats joining Republicans; the bill now goes to President Trump's desk.
  • The package authorises Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top importers of Russian oil and gas — putting India, China and others directly in the crosshairs — and targets Russia's energy sector, financial institutions and its "shadow fleet" of tankers.
  • Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that the new US sanctions would fall "under the category of unfriendly actions" and "would certainly complicate efforts to find a peace settlement in Ukraine."
  • India has already warned Washington that new tariffs over Russian oil purchases could damage bilateral ties.

The US House of Representatives on Wednesday gave final approval to a sweeping sanctions package aimed at squeezing Russia's war economy, passing the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 by a 262-159 vote and sending it to President Donald Trump for his signature — a move the Kremlin immediately warned would make a Ukraine peace deal harder to reach.

Named for the late Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, who died on July 11 after a year of shepherding the legislation, the bill is the most substantial American legislative effort on Ukraine since Trump returned to the White House. It cleared a procedural hurdle on Tuesday by 214-211, with two Democrats breaking ranks to advance it, and passed with dozens of Democrats voting in favour despite opposition from the party's senior leadership.

The Senate passed the measure last month by an overwhelming 86-11. Getting the package to Trump's desk required integrating the president's demand for a five-year extension of existing sanctions on Iran.

What the bill does

The legislation targets Russia's energy and defence industries, Russian financial institutions and the "shadow fleet" of tankers Moscow uses to evade existing Western limits on oil shipments, in order to deprive the Kremlin of revenue to finance the war.

Its most consequential — and most contested — provision gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the largest importers of Russian petroleum and natural gas, aimed at pressuring countries to cut their dependence on Russian energy. The Senate-passed version referred to the five largest importers by volume; a House amendment proposed by Democratic Congressman Steny Hoyer would explicitly name ten countries as eligible for the duties — China, India, Turkiye, Azerbaijan, Hungary, the Slovak Republic, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Kazakhstan and the Kyrgyz Republic. The amendment would not itself impose tariffs, but would identify India as eligible if the legislation is enacted and Trump exercises the authority.

Under the legislation, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer would determine the final tariff level — a guardrail that has not allayed concerns among lawmakers on both sides that the bill hands the White House a broad new tariff weapon.

Context and background

The bill's journey to passage was unusually tortuous. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy lobbied lawmakers directly ahead of the vote, telling them that "during the war, it is sometimes better to make a not-so-perfect decision than to do nothing." Republican Representative Michael McCaul, a lead sponsor, argued the moment demanded pressure: "Putin believes he can keep financing this war indefinitely. We need to change that calculation and ensure there are consequences for helping him."

"Putin believes he can keep financing this war indefinitely. We need to change that calculation and ensure there are consequences for helping him."

— Rep. Michael McCaul, lead sponsor of the bill

Opposition came from both ends. Representative Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, contended the bill grants Trump unchecked tariff authority, arguing that "White House lawyers drafted the current text to maximize President Trump's authority to impose new import taxes on the American people." Nearly a dozen Republicans privately lobbied Speaker Mike Johnson to strip the tariff provisions, alarmed that price hikes could hit just ahead of November's midterm elections — but Johnson and his leadership team rebuffed the proposed changes. Some non-interventionist Republicans opposed the sanctions entirely as contrary to an "America First" foreign policy.

The vote arrives with US-mediated peace efforts stalled for months. Trump sent two envoys to Moscow and Kyiv earlier this month in a bid to restart the process, after a parliamentary gridlock that had persisted for nearly two years following a 2024 emergency aid package for Ukraine.

Kremlin warns of 'complications'

The Kremlin responded on Thursday with a direct warning. "We are, of course, monitoring the progress of this document. It falls under the category of unfriendly actions, and of course the imposition of any additional sanctions by the U.S. would certainly complicate efforts to find a peace settlement in Ukraine," spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

"We are, of course, monitoring the progress of this document. It falls under the category of unfriendly actions, and of course the imposition of any additional sanctions by the U.S. would certainly complicate efforts to find a peace settlement in Ukraine."

— Dmitry Peskov, Kremlin spokesman

Impact on India

For India, the stakes are direct. New Delhi is among the largest buyers of discounted Russian crude, and the legislation creates a novel statutory pathway for Washington to impose tariffs of up to 100% on Indian imports in response. India has already warned Washington that new measures to levy tariffs over the purchase of Russian oil could impact bilateral ties, and the issue has become one of the most sensitive friction points in the relationship.

The diaspora will feel the downstream effects too: tariffs of that scale on Indian exports — from pharmaceuticals to textiles to electronics components — would land on businesses and consumers on both sides, while further straining the US-India trade negotiations already complicated by earlier tariff disputes.

What's next

The bill now heads to Trump's desk, where the decision to sign — and whether and how to use the tariff authorities — rests with the White House. USTR Jamieson Greer's eventual tariff determinations, if any, will show whether the secondary-tariff provisions become a live instrument or a pressure tactic. New Delhi, Beijing and other named importers will be watching the signing decision closely, and Indian officials are expected to press their case against any move that links energy purchases to punitive duties.
